Q: How to turn a string representation of a number in a given base back to a number? A:

You can use parseInt using a raidx 2. i.e

parseInt("1000", 2) will return 8

Q: PHP extending mysqli_result A:

You're getting the error because the $db->query($sql) returns a variable of type mysqli_result and not mysqli_result_extended. The mysqli_result class doesn't have a method named getJSON.

So when you define a class B that extends class A, it doesn't mean that all instances of the base class A magically become class B.

Q: Why does this function see only 2 values when I send an associative array and 3 values when I send a normal array? A:

Explaining the current behavior ...

This command requires the name of the array:

local -n parameter_names="$2"

The 1st time you call the function you should see $2 == normal_array, where normal_array is the valid name of an array.

The 2nd time you call the function you should see$2 == two, but two is not a valid array name so parameter_names ends up set to an empty array; which means "${parameter_names[@]}" generates nothing. The rest of "${!associative_array[@]}" (three and one) are processed as 'normal' input parameters (in this case they become the first 2 arguments after the shift 2 is processed).

You can see this behavior if you add the following:

aws_cli_flags+=("$@")

typeset -p parameter_names ${!parameter_names} aws_cli_flags    # new code

set -x

Running your code with the additional typeset -p call should generate:

declare -n parameter_names="normal_array"
declare -a normal_array=([0]="one" [1]="two" [2]="three")
declare -a aws_cli_flags=([0]="delete-parameters" [1]="--names" [2]="one"

... snip ...

declare -n parameter_names="two"
bash: typeset: two: not found
declare -a aws_cli_flags=([0]="delete-parameters" [1]="--names" [2]="three" [3]="one" [4]="--color" [5]="on")

And the output when passing the array name (associative_array) as an argument:

declare -n parameter_names="associative_array"
declare -A associative_array=([two]="value_two" [three]="value_three" [one]="value_one" )
declare -a aws_cli_flags=([0]="delete-parameters" [1]="--names" [2]="value_two" [3]="value_three" [4]="value_one" [5]="--color" [6]="on")

As for what you want to do (send array indices) ...

You'll need to modify your approach based on what you want to happen.

Assuming you still want to send the array name to the function, then in the function you would reference the (local) array's indices with:

${!parameter_names[@]}

After the typeset -p ... call add the following to demonstrate:

echo "parameter_names indices : ${!parameter_names[@]} :"

Which should generate the following lines of output (corresponding to the above snippets):

#####
# function called with 'normal_array'

parameter_names indices : 0 1 2 :

#####
# function called with '"${!associative_array[@]}"'
# NOTE: 'two' is an invalid array name so parameters_names[] is empty, hence no indices

parameter_names indices :  :

#####
# function called with 'associative_array'

parameter_names indices : two three one :

You'll need to decide if the function should process the array's indices or the array's values and code accordingly.

Q: Median of median algorithm recurrence relation A:

Best attempt:

That equation is only for when you do the median of groups of 5. Otherwise it will change. The an part of the equation is the time it takes for the algorithm to go through all the elements and group them into 5, as well as to find the median of each group of 5. The T(n/5) is the time it takes to find the median of these medians by making a recursive call on n/5 elements, as there are n/5 groups of 5.

T(7n/10) will take more time...

When you do the medians of medians the elements are broken up into 4 quadrants. 3/10 of the elements are greater than the median of medians, 3/10 elements are less than the median of medians. The other 4/10 is split up unto 2 groups of 2/10. These are the elements in which you're not sure if they are greater or less than the median of medians. Therefore, the max number of elements you could have that are greater than or less than the median of medians is 3/10 + 2/10 + 2/10 = 7/10. So the T(7n/10) is the part of continuing the equation with the max segment of numbers that is larger/smaller than the median of medians....

Hopefully that kind of makes sense.

Q: Where does '.' and '..' come from? A:

Excerpt from an interview with Ken Thompson (9-6-89):

Every time we made a directory, by convention we put it in another directory called directory - directory, which was dd. Its name was dd and that all the users directories and in fact most other directories, users maintain their own directory systems, had pointers back to dd, and dd got shortened into ‘dot-dot,’ and dd was for directory-directory.

Q: Constant expression violates subrange bounds A:

Does char really ocuppy one byte of memory? I mean, check whether it is an "Ansi" single-byte char and not a WideChar.

Anyway, when you need to access the last index of an array, you'd better use

ForTolkResult[High(ForTolkResult)] := chr(0);
